title: Simplify, Order, Break, Repeat
abstract: Existing symmetry-breaking techniques for SAT constrain the search space without simplifying the formula. Lex-leader predicates, the most widely used approach, add global ordering constraints to remove symmetric solutions, but often at the cost of substantial formula blowup and large proofs. Moreover, they ignore structural properties of the formula, such as connectedness, that could enable stronger symmetry breaking. In this paper, we present a new algorithm that treats symmetry breaking not merely as a restriction mechanism, but as a simplification mechanism. Notably, it only adds unit and binary symmetry-breaking clauses, which enables strong formula simplifications. This can expose additional symmetries and in turn allows for multiple rounds of symmetry breaking. Crucially, we exploit connectivity in the formula’s graph representation, including the presence of cliques, to guide the order of symmetry breaking. We implemented our algorithm in the satsuma tool and evaluated it on a large set of benchmarks. As a preprocessing step for CaDiCaL, it improves PAR-2 scores by 22% on the SAT competition 2025 and by 12% on the SAT anniversary track. It also substantially outperforms lex-leader and orbitopal fixing while producing compact proofs.

      Abstract
Existing symmetry-breaking techniques for SAT constrain the search space without simplifying the
formula. Lex-leader predicates, the most widely used approach, add global ordering constraints to
remove symmetric solutions, but often at the cost of substantial formula blowup and large proofs.
Moreover, they ignore structural properties of the formula, such as connectedness, that could enable
stronger symmetry breaking. In this paper, we present a new algorithm that treats symmetry
breaking not merely as a restriction mechanism, but as a simplification mechanism. Notably, it only
adds unit and binary symmetry-breaking clauses, which enables strong formula simplifications. This
can expose additional symmetries and in turn allows for multiple rounds of symmetry breaking.
Crucially, we exploit connectivity in the formula’s graph representation, including the presence of
cliques, to guide the order of symmetry breaking. We implemented our algorithm in the satsuma
tool and evaluated it on a large set of benchmarks. As a preprocessing step for CaDiCaL, it improves
PAR-2 scores by 22% on the SAT competition 2025 and by 12% on the SAT anniversary track. It
also substantially outperforms lex-leader and orbitopal fixing while producing compact proofs.

 1      Introduction
Symmetries in Boolean satisfiability (SAT) instances can cause solvers to redundantly
explore equivalent regions of the search space, leading to significant performance degradation.
Symmetry breaking mitigates this problem by restricting the search space to asymmetric
solutions. This technique is effective on many highly symmetric benchmarks [1, 4, 17, 18],
and it has been integrated into a wide range of solver paradigms [21, 36]. Yet despite these
successes, symmetry breaking has not become a standard component of modern SAT solvers.
    The difficulty is largely algorithmic. Effective symmetry handling must balance prun-
ing strength against computational overhead, all without disrupting core solver heuristics.
Moreover, every symmetry-breaking inference must be justified by a formally checkable
proof [30], which constrains the kinds of symmetry reasoning that are admissible.
    Today, the most practical SAT symmetry-breaking tools add lex-leader constraints to the
formula, justified via the so-called dominance rule [3, 13]. This approach, however, suffers
from two significant drawbacks. First, the dominance rule is only supported by systems based

      on pseudo-Boolean reasoning, which empirically incur substantially higher proof generation
      and verification costs than standard clausal proofs. Second, lex-leader constraints tend to
      blow up the size of the formula, potentially offsetting their pruning benefits.
          Motivated by these shortcomings, recent work [5] introduced a new symmetry-breaking
      approach for SAT inspired by orbitopal fixing from mixed-integer programming [27]. This
      method adds only unit clauses to the formula, which avoids formula blowup, and it admits
      succinct proofs entirely within the substitution redundancy (sr) clausal proof system [16, 22],
      which integrates naturally with existing SAT proof infrastructures. These advantages,
      however, come at the cost of reduced pruning power: in its current form, orbitopal fixing
      is structurally more limited than lex-leader constraints and requires certain cardinality
      constraints to be present in the formula, restricting its applicability.
          This state of affairs reveals a fundamental tension at the heart of certified symmetry
      breaking in SAT: stronger pruning demands more expressive and more expensive proof
      systems, whereas the efficiency of clausal proofs currently means using weaker symmetry
      techniques. In this work, we investigate how far symmetry breaking can be pushed within
      the confines of the sr clausal proof system.

      Contribution. We present a new symmetry-breaking algorithm for certified SAT solving
      that combines ideas from orbitopal fixing [5], recent work on iterated Schreier-Sims table
      cuts [24], and standard CNF preprocessing techniques. At a high level, it looks like this:
       1. Simplify the formula using CNF preprocessing techniques.
       2. Compute the symmetries of the formula. If only trivial symmetries remain, terminate.
       3. Break detected symmetries by adding unit and binary clauses.
       4. Repeat from Step 1.
      Unlike lex-leader approaches, which add long structured encodings and new variables to the
      formula, our algorithm produces a formula that is usually smaller than the input. It also
      emits succinct sr proofs justifying the clauses it added.
          Our algorithm has three key features. First, because the algorithm only adds unit and
      binary clauses to the formula, the formula can be simplified using standard preprocessing
      techniques, which can in turn reveal new symmetries to break. Having multiple rounds
      of symmetry detection is unique among static symmetry-breaking techniques for SAT,1
      and is inspired by recent symmetry-handling techniques for stable set solvers [24]. Second,
      we take inspiration from successful graph coloring heuristics [23, 25] to guide the order in
      which we add symmetry-breaking clauses. In particular, we fix variables involved in cliques
      in the formula’s variable-clause graph. To find these cliques, we use the maximum-clique
      solver cliquer [38], along with some lightweight heuristics. Third, our algorithm uses the
      Schreier-Sims algorithm [32, 34] to introduce symmetry-breaking clauses. Compared to more
      common filtering-based heuristics [4, 18], this approach systematically generates clauses for a
      chosen pointwise stabilizer chain while allowing for more flexible variable orderings.
          Experimentally, our algorithm is quite effective. When implemented in the satsuma [4]
      symmetry-breaking tool and used as a preprocessing step for the state-of-the-art SAT
      solver CaDiCaL [11], our algorithm improves PAR-2 scores on benchmarks from the SAT
      anniversary track by 12% and the SAT Competition 2025 by 22%. It is also highly effective
      on a variety of crafted benchmarks, completely solving many of them during preprocessing.
      The preprocessing overhead is negligible, amounting to less than 1% of the average solve time.
      Overall, our algorithm outperforms previous work on orbitopal fixing symmetry breaking, as
      well as state-of-the-art lex-leader symmetry-breaking techniques.

 2     Preliminaries
We assume that the reader is generally familiar with concepts from SAT solving. For a
comprehensive introduction, please refer to the Handbook of Satisfiability [12].
    The propositional formulas in this paper are all in conjunctive normal form (CNF),
consisting of conjunctions of disjunctive clauses each containing Boolean literals. A literal ℓ
is either a Boolean variable x or its negation x.
    We interpret clauses as sets of literals and formulas as sets of clauses, meaning we may, for
example, write the clause (x ∨ y ∨ z) as {x, y, z}. We write Var(F ) and Lit(F ) to refer to the
variables and literals occurring in F , respectively. Two formulas F and F ′ are equisatisfiable
if F is satisfiable iff F ′ is satisfiable.
    Since cardinality constraints are used by both our algorithm and recent work on orbitopal
fixing in SAT [5], we define a couple of relevant notions here.
    First, a clause C is an AMO clause if all of its literals appear in a trivial at-most-one
(AMO) encoding in a given CNF F . In other words, C is an AMO clause if (ℓ1 ∨ ℓ2 ) ∈ F for
every pair of distinct literals ℓ1 , ℓ2 ∈ C. As a result, if any literal in C is set to true, then all
of the other literals in C are set to false under unit propagation.
    Second, a clause C ∈ F is a unique literal clause (ULC) with respect to F if none of its
literals appear elsewhere in F \ C. For ULCs, the following property holds.
▶ Lemma 1 ([33], Lemma 4). Let F be a formula, and let C ∈ F be a ULC. If F is satisfiable,
then it can be satisfied with exactly one literal in C assigned to true.
   A corollary of Lemma 1 is that we can transform any ULC C into an AMO clause by
adding the binary clauses (ℓ1 ∨ ℓ2 ) to F for every pair of distinct literals ℓ1 , ℓ2 ∈ C. Notably,
the addition of these clauses preserves the satisfiability of F .

2.1    Substitution Redundancy
All modern SAT solvers are certifying algorithms [30], meaning they produce answers that
can be checked by formally-verified software. In the satisfiable case, the solver returns a
truth assignment τ , and it is trivial to check whether τ satisfies the formula. The more
interesting case is when the formula is unsatisfiable. Today, the de facto standard is for the
solver to emit a proof of unsatisfiability in a clausal proof system. The most popular format
is drat [37], based on the rat proof system [26]. In this paper, we use the substitution
redundancy (sr) proof system [15, 16, 22, 31], which is a generalization of rat.
    Clausal proofs comprise a series of addition and deletion steps. Each addition step
adds a redundant clause C to the formula F , where C is redundant if F and (F ∧ C) are
equisatisfiable. Addition steps may also include a witness ω that helps show the redundancy
of C. In sr, witnesses are substitutions ω : Var(F ) → Lit(F ) ∪ {⊤, ⊥} mapping variables to
literals or to fixed truth values. Substitutions extend to literals in the natural way.
    To show that a clause C is redundant, it suffices to show that it is substitution redundant.
▶ Definition 2 (Substitution redundant [16]). A clause C is substitution redundant for a
formula F if there exists a witness ω such that F ∧ ¬C ⊢1 (F ∧ C)|ω , where ¬C := ∧ℓ∈C ℓ
and where F |ω means substituting each literal of F with its image under ω.
    Intuitively, the witness ω repairs any assignment τ that satisfies F but not C into an
assignment that satisfies both. The sr rule uses unit propagation ⊢1 rather than general
entailment ⊨ because unit propagation is efficiently checkable by a proof checker.
    Today, only the dsr/lsr [16] and VeriPB [22] proof formats support the sr rule. The
implementation of our algorithm in satsuma can produce proofs in either format.

      2.2    Symmetry in SAT
      A symmetry of a formula F is a permutation of Lit(F ) that maps F back to itself. Formally,
      let σ be a permutation of Lit(F ), and let σ(F ) be the formula obtained by relabeling the
      literals of F under σ. Then σ is a syntactic symmetry of F if:
       1. σ(F ) = F , and
       2. σ commutes with negation, i.e., ¬σ(ℓ) = σ(ℓ) for all ℓ ∈ Lit(F ).
      The set of all symmetries of F together with the composition operation ◦ forms a permutation
      group, denoted Aut(F ). We write Γ′ ≤ Γ if Γ′ is a subgroup of a permutation group Γ,
      meaning that Γ′ ⊆ Γ and Γ′ is also a permutation group.
          In this paper, we use two standard group-theoretic notions: stabilizers and orbits. The
      orbit of a literal ℓ in a permutation group Γ is the set of literals reachable from ℓ using
      permutations of Γ. Formally, the orbit of ℓ in Γ is defined as OΓ (ℓ) := {σ(ℓ) | σ ∈ Γ}.
          Given a set of literals L, the pointwise stabilizer Γ(L) is the set of permutations in Γ
      mapping every literal ℓ ∈ L to itself. Formally, we define:

         Γ(L) := {σ ∈ Γ | σ(ℓ) = ℓ for all ℓ ∈ L}.

      Observe that Γ(L) ≤ Γ holds. If L = {ℓ} contains a single literal, we will write Γ(ℓ) .

      2.3    Orbitopal Fixing
      Orbitopal fixing [5, 9, 27] is a symmetry-breaking technique first studied by the mixed-integer
      programming community. It derives unit clauses from a matrix of literals containing row
      symmetry [19] and certain cardinality constraints. In the SAT setting, the derivation of these
      unit clauses is justified with short sr proofs [5]. In Section 4.3, we discuss how we optimized
      this technique as a sub-procedure for our preprocessing algorithm.

           If both of these conditions are met, then we may derive the unit clauses (ℓn,1 ) and

      requires detecting row symmetries. Nevertheless, matrix symmetry is a standard notion in
      symmetry handling [19], and heuristic techniques for discovering such structures are common
      in practical symmetry-breaking systems [4, 9, 18]. Once a matrix with row symmetry is found,
      checking whether each column is a ULC of F is straightforward, especially since the set of
      ULCs in a formula can be computed in linear time [33].

 3      Schreier-Sims Table Cuts
A popular technique for symmetry handling is deriving Schreier-Sims table cuts [1, 18, 24, 29].
In this section, we adapt this technique to iterative symmetry breaking for SAT, and we
show that it is correct and that it admits short sr proofs.
   Let us start with its definition. Schreier-Sims table cuts are binary clauses systematically
derived from a chain of pointwise stabilizers.

▶ Definition 3 (SST cuts). Let F be a CNF formula, and let Γ ≤ Aut(F ) be a subgroup of
the symmetries of F . For a literal ℓ ∈ Lit(F ), the Schreier–Sims table cuts (SST cuts) of F
at ℓ are the set of binary clauses:

     SSTΓ (ℓ) := {(ℓ ∨ ℓ′ ) | ℓ′ ∈ OΓ (ℓ), ℓ′ ̸= ℓ}.

Intuitively, the clauses in SSTΓ (ℓ) enforce that if ℓ is set to true, then all literals in its orbit
must also be set to true. In other words, ℓ is the smallest literal in its orbit. An analogous
definition is also possible where the binary clauses (ℓ ∨ ℓ′ ) make ℓ the largest literal in its
orbit, but unless otherwise stated, we use the definition above.
    Following the proof strategy for clausal fixing due to Anders et al. [5], we prove that
adding the clauses in SSTΓ (ℓ) to the formula preserves satisfiability and admits an sr proof.

▶ Theorem 4. Let F be a CNF formula and Γ ≤ Aut(F ). Then the following hold:
1. F and F ∧ SSTΓ (ℓ) are equisatisfiable.
2. There is an sr proof deriving F ∧ SSTΓ (ℓ) from F in | SSTΓ (ℓ)| steps.

Proof. (1). Let τ be an assignment satisfying F but not F ∧ SSTΓ (ℓ). Then there is a clause
{ℓ, ℓ′ } ∈ SSTΓ (ℓ) which is falsified by τ , meaning τ assigns ℓ to true and ℓ′ to false.
     By the definition of Schreier cuts, ℓ′ ∈ OΓ (ℓ) holds. Hence, there exists a symmetry σ
with σ(ℓ) = ℓ′ . Using this symmetry, we obtain a new assignment τ ′ = τ ◦ σ that sets ℓ
to false. Then τ ′ satisfies F ∧ SSTΓ (ℓ): it satisfies all clauses in SSTΓ (ℓ), since each clause
contains ℓ, and it satisfies F , since σ is a syntactic symmetry of F and τ satisfies F .
     (2). The sr proof derives in an arbitrary order the clauses {ℓ, ℓ′ } with ℓ′ ∈ OΓ (ℓ) and
ℓ′ ̸= ℓ. Each clause {ℓ, ℓ′ } has as witness the symmetry ω ∈ Γ mapping ω(ℓ) = ℓ′ . Suppose

    SST cuts are usually added in multiple rounds: they are added for a literal ℓ, then
the symmetries Γ are reduced to the pointwise stabilizer Γ(ℓ) and the process is repeated.
Intuitively, this process constructs a lexicographic ordering on the literals, where each new
literal ℓ is placed after all previously fixed literals but before all other remaining literals.
    However, because sr proofs have no notion of lexicographic order, we must use a different
argument to prove that restricting the symmetries to Γ(ℓ) allows us to iteratively apply SST
cuts while still generating sr proofs. Fortunately, stabilizing ℓ yields syntactic symmetries of
the newly enriched formula. Thus, the symmetries in Γ(ℓ) continue to be valid sr witnesses
in the resulting formula. We prove this formally in the following lemma.

 4      Iterated Preprocessing
We now describe our new preprocessing algorithm for symmetry handling in SAT. We begin
by describing the high-level routine, followed by more detailed descriptions of the involved
subroutines and heuristics.

4.1     Preprocessing Algorithm
Algorithm 1 outlines our core routine at a high level. We implement it in satsuma [4].

     Algorithm 1 A high-level description of our preprocessing algorithm.
 1   function preprocess
           Input : ➢ CNF formula F
         Output : ➢ CNF formula F ′ equisatisfiable to F
                   ➢ sr proof
 2      while true do
 3        // simplify and enrich F
 4        propagate unit and pure literals in F ;
 5        merge equivalent literals in F ;
 6        remove duplicate literals and duplicate/tautological clauses in F ;
 7        add AMO binary clauses over the ULCs in F ;
 8          // compute symmetries of F
 9          Γ := Aut(F );
10          if |Γ| = 1 then return F ;
11          // apply symmetry-handling routines
12          (F, Γ) := orbitopal-fixing(F, Γ);
13          (F, Γ) := negation-fixing(F, Γ);
14          (F, Γ) := fix-and-cut(F, Γ);



Description. The algorithm begins by simplifying the formula F . First, it propagates
unit and pure literals (i.e., literals whose negations do not appear in F ). Next, pairs of
equivalent literals x and y are merged, where x and y are equivalent if they imply each other,
meaning (x ∨ y), (x ∨ y) ∈ F . All occurrences of x and y in F are replaced with a canonical
representative. Then, all tautological clauses, duplicate clauses, and duplicate literals in
clauses are removed. Finally, AMO binary clauses are added for all ULC clauses in F .
    Once the formula F is simplified, the symmetries of F are computed. If F contains no
nontrivial symmetries, the algorithm terminates. Otherwise, symmetry-handling routines are
applied in the order of (1) orbitopal fixing (Section 4.3), (2) negation fixing [5], and (3)
a fix-and-cut routine applying Schreier-Sims table cuts and clausal fixing [5] (Section 4.2).
Orbitopal fixing is applied first, since subsequent routines may destroy the conditions required
for its application. The algorithm loops from there, alternating between formula simplification
and symmetry breaking until termination or until practical limits are reached.
    Regarding the choice of CNF preprocessing techniques, any equisatisfiable preprocessing
method could be incorporated into the algorithm. However, because the algorithm exploits
symmetries after preprocessing, it is preferable to use techniques that preserve as much useful
symmetry as possible. Indeed, standard preprocessing methods such as bounded variable
elimination and self-subsumption can destroy useful symmetries [2].

      Correctness. The algorithm maintains the invariants that F is equisatisfiable to the original
      input formula and that Γ ≤ Aut(F ) holds. Note that since F and Γ may change throughout

      Implementation. Similar to prior work [5], orbitopal fixing is applied using the structure
      detection of satsuma, which means the symmetries are not computed all at once. Rather,
      for the purpose of orbitopal fixing, only the relevant structured symmetries are computed,
      while the remaining symmetries are computed afterwards. This leads to a small optimization:
      if orbitopal fixing adds unit clauses to the formula, we can immediately restart the loop
      and simplify the formula again (since, after orbitopal fixing, we have not yet computed any
      symmetries not involved in the structures used for orbitopal fixing).
          Furthermore, in practice we limit the maximum number of iterations, where larger
      formulas F have smaller iteration budgets. However, this limit depends on the current size
      of F , so if F shrinks during execution, the allowed number of iterations increases.

Description. Given a formula F and a subgroup of its symmetries Γ ≤ Aut(F ), the
procedure iteratively adds symmetry-breaking clauses to F using SST cuts and clausal fixing.
The algorithm maintains a set S of variables that have already been fixed or used for SST
cuts. It repeats the following until Γ becomes trivial (i.e., |Γ| = 1).
    In each iteration, the algorithm chooses a literal ℓ that breaks the most symmetries. First,
it looks for an AMO clause C that admits clausal fixing, meaning that C ⊆ OΓ (ℓ) for some
ℓ ∈ C. If such a clause exists, then the algorithm fixes an arbitrary literal ℓ ∈ C to true,
which causes all other literals in C to be set to false. If no such AMO clause exists, then
the algorithm selects a candidate literal ℓ with nontrivial orbit that has the highest number
of shared clauses C ∈ F with var(ℓ) ∈ Var(C) and var(ℓ′ ) ∈ Var(C) for some ℓ′ ∈ S. (In
practice, if multiple literals have the same number of shared clauses, the algorithm prefers
literals that admit clausal fixing.) Intuitively, literals with many shared clauses are often
closely related in the formula, so focusing on them tends to break symmetries in the same
part of the problem. In Section 5.2, we experimentally study the effects of using this order.
    Once a candidate literal ℓ is selected, the algorithm tries to apply clausal fixing. If
there exists a clause C with ℓ ∈ C such that C ⊆ OΓ (ℓ), then the algorithm adds the unit
clause {ℓ}. Otherwise, the algorithm adds SST cuts for ℓ.
    After adding either unit clauses or SST cuts, the subgroup Γ is updated to the pointwise
stabilizer Γ(ℓ) , ℓ is recorded in S, and the loop repeats until termination.

Correctness. All clause additions are valid due to Theorem 4, and the update of Γ to
Γ(ℓ) ≤ Aut(F ′ ) is valid due to Lemma 5. In other words, the resulting formula F ′ is
equisatisfiable to F , and the resulting group of symmetries Γ is a subgroup of Aut(F ′ ).

Implementation. The pointwise stabilizers are implemented using a random Schreier-Sims
algorithm, as provided by the dejavu library [6, 7]. In practice, this routine is subject to
a modest size limit and is invoked only when the domain size (i.e., the number of involved
literals) of Γ is at most 100 000. Furthermore, the Schreier-Sims algorithm is applied with a
heuristic cost limit based on the approximate number of operations performed. As a fallback
mechanism, we use a cheap filtering heuristic.
    The random Schreier-Sims algorithm also helps produce the sr proofs. The algorithm
maintains a so-called transversal for each stabilized literal ℓ. Conceptually, the transversal
associates each literal ℓ′ in the orbit of ℓ with a symmetry σ such that σ(ℓ′ ) = ℓ. (In practice,
these symmetries are represented implicitly via Schreier vectors [32].) The required sr
witnesses are extracted directly from these transversals.
    However, there’s a delicate detail when using the random Schreier-Sims algorithm to
produce sr proofs. The algorithm may, due to randomness, return orbits that are smaller
than the actual orbit of some literal ℓ. These erroneous orbits might get repaired in subsequent
calls to the algorithm (perhaps when fixing another literal ℓ′ ), but this means that when we
fix ℓ, we might not add all of the necessary binary clauses for ℓ. While this can never lead to
deriving incorrect clauses, the sr proof may lack some of the clauses necessary for iterated
SST cut applications, as required by Lemma 5.
    We avoid this issue by implementing a two-pass algorithm: We first decide which fix-and-
cut routines are going to be applied, and then we use one consistent call to the Schreier-Sims
algorithm to produce the actual constraints and sr proof.
    We end with two small implementation notes. First, rather than simplifying the formula
after each loop, we perform the overlap test C ⊆ OΓ (ℓ) on Line 11 with C reduced under S.
Second, the implementation of negation fixing in Algorithm 1 is a special case of Algorithm 2.
The algorithm simply chooses literals ℓ with ℓ ∈ OΓ (ℓ) until no more remain.

       4.3        Clique-guided Orbitopal Fixing
       Lastly, we describe a heuristic optimization for the orbitopal fixing rule (Section 2.3). Assume
       we can apply orbitopal fixing to a matrix M . Since the rows of M are fully symmetric,
       their ordering is of no importance to the algorithm. However, the columns of M need not
       be symmetric to each other, meaning they may be structurally distinct and encode vastly
       different things in the underlying formula. This matters because, in orbitopal fixing, all
       literals of the first column of M are fixed, all but two literals of the second column are fixed,
       all but three literals of the third column are fixed, and so on. Thus, the ordering of the
       columns may significantly affect how powerful the symmetry breaking is.
           Given this observation, our heuristic reorders the columns of M based on finding cliques
       in the graph extracted from M and the formula F . Our motivation stems from graph coloring:
       If the number of colors (i.e., rows) is smaller than the size of the clique, then by moving the
       clique’s columns to the front of M and applying orbitopal fixing, we immediately solve the
       graph coloring instance (i.e., orbitopal fixing propagates to conflict on the clique).

    5      Experimental Results

We implemented our techniques in satsuma2 and evaluated them on three benchmark
families: (1) the anniversary track of the SAT Competition 2022 [8], comprising 5344 distinct,
non-random instances from the SAT Competitions 2002 to 2021, (2) the main track of the
SAT Competition 2025, comprising 386 formulas, and (3) a collection of highly symmetric
synthetic instances that have appeared in various papers on symmetry breaking, comprising
236 formulas representing Tseitin graphs, clique and graph coloring problems, instances
from Ramsey theory, counting principle problems, channel routing problems, and several
variants of the pigeonhole problem. We generated many of them using CNFgen [28], and
the two pigeons per hole (tph) family is due to Biere [10]. For the anniversary and 2025
suites, we filtered out all formulas that were trivially unsatisfiable (i.e., formulas containing
the empty clause) and all formulas larger than 1 GB in size, since these formulas exceed
internal computational limits in satsuma, meaning satsuma would not attempt to symmetry
break them anyway. Removing these instances also prevents memouts while running the
experiments.

       5.1     Main Results
       The summary statistics can be found in Table 1. Overall, our new iterated algorithm has
       the best PAR-2 scores across all three benchmark suites, and it also performs the best on
       many synthetic sub-families. For all variations of satsuma, average preprocessing time is
       less than 1% of the average solve time. Looking inside the competition suites: On the SAT
       Competition 2025, our algorithm wins over base CaDiCaL on instances from Ramsey theory
       and scheduling problems, as well as crafted benchmarks from clique coloring, pigeonhole, and

 6     Conclusions and Future Work
In conclusion, we introduced a new symmetry-breaking algorithm for certified SAT solving that
combines orbitopal fixing, iterated Schreier-Sims table cuts, and standard CNF preprocessing.
When evaluated on a wide selection of benchmarks, our algorithm achieves substantial
speedup with negligible overhead. Surprisingly, it clearly outperforms prior symmetry-
breaking techniques while producing succinct sr proofs. In particular, many instances are
solved completely within the new algorithm.
    We hope that our approach can serve as a blueprint for future developments in efficient
symmetry-handling algorithms for SAT. Indeed, several interesting directions still remain:
    Incorporate more powerful symmetry-preserving [2] CNF preprocessing techniques, to be
    used in between rounds of symmetry breaking.
    Raise the practical limits by making the involved algorithms more efficient.
    Design and evaluate more ordering heuristics.
